transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for taking the time to see me. I, uh, I suppose what brings me in today is... well, it's actually been going on for a little while now, but it's gotten to the point where it's just becoming a real nuisance. We live in a condo over on the east side, and lately, I just find myself... I get stuck, I suppose is the best way to put it. 

I find myself checking things over and over again before I can move on with my day. It’s always the same things, too. I have these boxes in the spare room, and my daily to-do lists, and, well, just the regular drawers around the condo—the kitchen drawers, the dresser, that sort of thing. I'll open one up, look inside, close it, and then... I just have to do it again. I'll open it right back up. And the ridiculous thing is, I know perfectly well I already looked. My memory is fine, I know exactly what's in there and what isn't. But I just can't seem to walk away until I've checked it a few more times. 

My wife will be standing right there by the front door, coat on, just waiting for me to leave it be so we can go out to the store or run our errands, and I'll be standing there pulling the same drawer open for the third or fourth time. I tell her, "Just a minute, just a minute," but it's never just a minute, you know? I just have to do it, even though I know I just looked. It's just very frustrating to deal with, frankly, and she's the one who finally suggested I come talk to someone about it.
Do you have any disturbing or intrusive thoughts that keep repeating in your mind?

Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, that's exactly what happens. It's... it's a very nagging sort of feeling, and it just won't leave me be. 

You see, I was a teacher for many years before I retired—middle school, mostly—and over the decades I accumulated quite a lot of materials. I kept a good number of my old teaching files, because, well, you put a lot of work into those things and you just never know what you might want to look back on. But lately, I keep getting these thoughts... these incredibly persistent thoughts that I might have accidentally thrown away something important from those old files. 

Or it happens with my tools, too. We downsized to the condo, so I only kept a small set of tools for minor repairs, hanging pictures, that sort of thing. And I'll suddenly get this thought stuck in my head that I've put a needed tool in the wrong box. I'll be sitting down in my favorite chair—my wife and I usually like to watch a bit of television or read after dinner—and I'll tell myself, "Now, that is highly unlikely. You haven't even touched those teaching files in months, and you know exactly where the hammer is." 

I try to just reason with myself, you know? Because I know it doesn't make logical sense. But even when I tell myself it's unlikely, the thought just comes right back. It just loops around and around in my mind, and it makes it terribly hard to settle down and just enjoy the evening. I'll be sitting there, trying to focus on a book or the program on the screen, and my mind is just absolutely stuck on whether or not a piece of paper from twenty years ago got tossed in the recycling by mistake. It just chatters away at me until I finally get up and go check on it.
Do you feel like things need to be in a certain order or symmetrical for you to feel comfortable?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I like a tidy house, certainly. We both do. When we downsized and moved into the condo, my wife—she has a wonderful eye for these things, you see—she arranged the living room so nicely, with the armchairs angled just so, and the little side tables matching. But if, say, one of our grandkids comes over to visit and bumps a lamp out of place, or if the coasters on the coffee table aren't perfectly lined up, it doesn't bother me in the slightest. 

I don't get that... that nagging feeling about things being uneven or out of order. It's really just the checking of the boxes and the drawers that I mentioned earlier. I can leave a stack of mail completely askew on the kitchen counter, and as long as I don't have that specific thought that an important paper got accidentally tossed out, I'm perfectly fine leaving it a mess. 

So, no, it doesn't have to be symmetrical or anything like that. I've heard of people who need all their soup cans facing forward in the pantry, or their shoes lined up perfectly by the door, but I've never been quite like that. In fact, if you had seen my desk back when I was teaching middle school, you'd probably laugh—it was a bit of a disaster area, honestly, just stacks of ungraded quizzes and lesson plans everywhere! But I always knew where everything was, at least back then. So, no, the physical arrangement or symmetry of things isn't what's bothering me at all. It's really just those persistent thoughts about misplacing or throwing away something important.
Do you feel like checking these things repeatedly is preventing something bad from happening?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's not as if I think... oh, I don't know, that the condo is going to catch fire, or that someone in the family is going to fall ill if I don't look in the drawer. It's nothing dramatic like that. My wife actually asked me something very similar just the other week. We were getting ready to head over to the grocery store—the one down on 4th street, they have those wonderful fresh bakery items on Tuesday mornings—and I was stuck checking the hall table drawer. She sighed and asked me, "What on earth do you think is going to happen if you don't look in there again?" And I had to tell her, honestly, nothing! Nothing bad is going to happen at all. 

It's really just... well, it's just about the items themselves. It's that nagging feeling I mentioned before. If I don't check, I just sit there feeling like I've made a foolish mistake. Like I've carelessly tossed out a perfectly good wrench, or one of those old teaching rubrics I spent hours typing up back in the nineties. It's just this incredibly frustrating sense of... of uncertainty, I suppose. I just want to be absolutely, one hundred percent sure that I haven't made an error. 

So I wouldn't say I'm preventing a catastrophe or anything terrible. It's just that if I don't go back and look, that thought—that I might have misplaced something—just gets louder and louder until I can't concentrate on a single other thing. I'll just be sitting there stewing over it. I just have to see the item with my own eyes to prove to myself that it's still there, even though, as I said, I already know it is! It's quite the paradox, really, when you think about it. But no, no impending doom or anything of that sort. Just trying to quiet my own mind, I suppose.
Do you feel less anxious after you've checked these things repeatedly?

Well... you know, it's funny you ask that, because it's not quite as simple as just feeling less anxious. I mean, yes, in the immediate moment, there is a certain... relief, I suppose you could call it. It's like scratching an itch. When I finally get up from my chair—which is quite a comfortable chair, mind you, a nice leather recliner my daughter got me for my seventieth birthday—and I walk over to the closet or the filing cabinet, and I actually lay my eyes on the hammer or the old lesson plans... yes, the nagging thought stops for a moment. 

But the relief, it's so incredibly fleeting. It's almost frustrating how short-lived it is. Because I'll close the drawer, feeling like, "Okay, good, it's there, I didn't throw it away." And I'll walk back to the living room. But sometimes, before I've even sat back down, or maybe five minutes after I pick my book back up, the thought just creeps right back in. "Are you sure you saw it? Maybe it was a different file. Maybe you just imagined seeing the hammer." 

So, I wouldn't say I feel *less anxious* overall. If anything, the whole process is exhausting. I'll check it, feel a tiny bit better for a split second, and then the doubt just washes right back over me. It's like trying to bail out a leaky boat with a teaspoon. You think you're making progress, but the water just keeps coming back in. So, no, the checking doesn't really fix the anxiety in any meaningful way. It just sort of... pauses it for a second before the whole cycle starts up again.
Do you think that if you could stop checking these things, your anxiety would decrease?

Oh, goodness... well, that is a... that's a rather difficult question to answer, isn't it? Because, you see, I'm honestly not sure. I really don't know. My wife is always telling me—just last week we were sitting down to watch a program, one of those wonderful Ken Burns documentaries on PBS, the one about the National Parks, which is just stunningly filmed by the way, you really ought to see it if you haven't—and I had this sudden thought that I had accidentally tossed the electric bill into the recycling bin along with the weekly grocery circulars. 

And she said to me, "Just sit here. Don't go look. Just ignore it and it will pass." So I tried. I really did try to just stop checking, right then and there. But... would the anxiety decrease if I could somehow permanently stop? I just don't know, because in that moment, sitting there trying not to check, the worry just built up and built up. It was like a kettle on the stove, just getting hotter and hotter until it whistles. I couldn't focus on the television screen at all, couldn't hear a single word the narrator was saying about Yosemite. I just kept picturing that bill sitting in the blue bin out in the garage, getting ruined. 

So, if I were somehow magically able to just stop doing the checking altogether... I don't know if my mind would finally quiet down and I'd feel peaceful, or if I'd just be sitting in my armchair vibrating with all that pent-up uncertainty all day long. It's a bit of a mystery to me, frankly, because I've never actually been able to hold out long enough to find out! I always end up getting up and looking eventually, just to break the tension. So, yes, I really couldn't say for certain one way or the other what would happen if I just stopped.
Do you think the things you check for could potentially cause harm if they were missing or misplaced?

Well, no, not really. I mean, harm? No, no, it's nothing like that. It's not as if I think someone is going to get hurt, or the house is going to collapse because I can't find a particular socket wrench or a stack of old papers. It's really just... well, it's just the principle of the thing, I suppose. 

Take those old lesson plans, for example. The ones I was telling you about from the nineties. Now, I haven't taught a class in over a decade, and I certainly don't have any pressing need for a rubric on a sophomore history essay about the Industrial Revolution. But the thought of it just being gone... of me having accidentally thrown it away without realizing it... it just feels like such a foolish, careless mistake. It's not dangerous, it's just... it's just wrong. 

And it's the same with the tools. My wife—she's a saint, really, putting up with me—she'll say, "Arthur, if you really need a Phillips head screwdriver that badly, we can just go down to the Ace Hardware on Main Street and buy another one for three dollars." And she's absolutely right, of course she is. It wouldn't be the end of the world. It wouldn't cause any harm to anyone. But in my mind, it's just this nagging, persistent feeling that I've lost something perfectly good, something I might need someday, however unlikely that is. It's the uncertainty of it all, the feeling of not being completely in control of my own belongings. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm worried about any sort of harm or danger. It's just... well, it's just incredibly bothersome, is what it is.
Do you feel like you're trying to prevent a mistake from happening when you check these things repeatedly?

Well, yes and no, I suppose. It's... it's a bit complicated. I mean, yes, on some level, I suppose I am trying to prevent a mistake—the mistake of having thrown something away or misplaced it. But really, what brought me in to see you in the first place, what finally made me realize I needed to talk to someone, is just the sheer repetition of it all. 

It's the fact that I find myself checking the exact same boxes in the garage, the same lists I've made for myself, the same drawers in our condo... over and over and over again. And the absurd part, the part that really gets under my skin, is that I know perfectly well I already looked! I have the memory of looking. I know the hammer is in the drawer, or the papers are in the box. But my brain just won't accept it. 

Just the other day, we were supposed to be going out to lunch with my wife's sister—Helen, lovely woman, lives over in the next town—and my wife was standing by the front door, purse in hand, just waiting for me. And I knew she was waiting. I knew we were going to be late. But I just couldn't leave it be. I had to go back into the guest room and check the filing cabinet one more time, just to be absolutely certain I hadn't accidentally mixed up the tax documents with the old lesson plans. I knew I hadn't. But I had to look. So it's less about preventing a mistake in the future, and more about... just needing to satisfy this terrible, repetitive urge before I can physically allow myself to move on with my day, even when I know it's completely unnecessary and I'm keeping my poor wife waiting.
Do you think your checking behavior is more about avoiding the feeling of uncertainty or the feeling of having made a mistake?

Well, I suppose it’s a bit of both, isn't it? But if I had to really put my finger on it, it's... it's the uncertainty that just gnaws at me. The uncertainty that I might have made a mistake. It’s this... this incessant, nagging thought that just pops into my head, usually right when I'm trying to relax. 

Just yesterday, for instance, I was sitting in my favorite armchair—it’s a wonderful old leather thing, terribly comfortable, my wife wanted to throw it out when we moved into the condo but I simply wouldn't let her—anyway, I was sitting there, reading the morning paper, and suddenly the thought just arrives out of nowhere: "Arthur, did you accidentally toss out that file on the 1994 curriculum changes?" 

Now, I know, logically, I haven't looked at that file in years. I know it’s highly unlikely I would have even had it out of the filing cabinet, let alone thrown it away. But the thought just... sticks. It’s like a burr caught in your sock when you’re out for a walk in the woods. You try to ignore it, you try to just keep walking, but it just keeps pricking at you. 

I tell myself, "Arthur, don't be ridiculous, it's fine." But the thought just circles back around. Or I'll think, "Did I put that good socket wrench in the box with the gardening supplies instead of the toolbox?" And even though I know I wouldn't do something so silly, I just can't settle down. I can't finish reading my article on the local mayoral race, I can't enjoy my cup of tea... because the thought just keeps echoing, over and over, until I finally give in and go out to the garage to check. So yes, it’s those nagging thoughts, that terrible uncertainty that I might have done something foolish with my old teaching files or my tools, that just makes it utterly impossible to sit still and be at peace.
Is it the possibility of having made a mistake that bothers you, or is it not knowing for sure whether everything is in its place?

Well, it's... it's a bit of both, I suppose, but the core of the issue, the part that really drives me to distraction, is that I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files, or perhaps put a needed tool in the wrong box out in the garage. And I know, I sit there in my armchair—the leather one I mentioned—and I tell myself it's highly unlikely. I say, "Arthur, you haven't touched the 1998 syllabus for the European History course in fifteen years, why on earth would you have thrown it out today?" Or I'll think about the crescent wrench, the good one with the rubber grip, and I'll tell myself there's absolutely no reason it would be in the box with the old Christmas ornaments. 

But the thought just comes back. It just loops around in my mind, over and over again, and it makes it terribly hard to just settle down. I try to read, I try to watch a bit of television with my wife, but the question is just there, hovering: "What if you did make a mistake? What if it's not where it's supposed to be?" And even though I know, logically, that everything is probably exactly where I left it, that little seed of doubt, that tiny "what if," just grows and grows until I simply cannot sit still anymore. I have to know for sure. I just have to.
Do you feel like checking these things repeatedly helps you regain a sense of control over your surroundings?

Well, control... I suppose you could use that word, but honestly, it doesn't really feel like control. It feels more like being controlled, if I'm being perfectly frank. Because, as I was saying earlier—and this is really the crux of the matter, the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment—what brought me in is that I find myself checking the exact same boxes out in the garage, the same lists I've jotted down, the same drawers in the condo, over and over again. 

And it's not a calm, in-control sort of feeling. It's a compulsion. I'll be standing there, looking at the drawer where we keep the spare keys and the batteries, and I'll check it, and then I'll close it, and then... I just can't move on. I have to open it again. And again. Even though, as I said, I know perfectly well I already looked! I can see the batteries in my mind's eye. But I just can't walk away. 

It's terribly frustrating, especially when it affects my wife. Like that time with Helen, waiting by the door. My wife is such a patient woman, truly, she puts up with so much of my nonsense, but even she has her limits. She'll be standing there, coat on, purse ready, just waiting for me to leave it be. "Arthur, come along, it's fine," she'll say. And I want to leave it be. I desperately want to just walk out the door and go to lunch and have a nice afternoon. But I can't. I have to check just one more time before my brain will physically allow me to move on to the next thing. So no, it doesn't feel like regaining control at all. It feels like being stuck in a loop that I can't break out of, no matter how much I want to or how much I know it's completely irrational.
Is the feeling of uncertainty about whether something is in its place more bothersome to you than the possibility of having actually made a mistake?

Well, it’s… I suppose it’s the uncertainty, but it’s really the thought itself that’s the bother. The thought of the mistake, the thought of the misplaced item, it just… it won’t leave me be. I keep getting these nagging thoughts, you see, that I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files. Or, as I mentioned, that I’ve put a needed tool in the wrong box out in the garage. 

And it’s so frustrating because I know better! I’ll be sitting there, and I’ll tell myself, "Arthur, it is highly unlikely you threw away the grade book from 1982." I know it’s unlikely. I tell myself it’s unlikely. But the thought just comes back anyway. It just pushes its way back in, no matter how much logic I throw at it. And it makes it so terribly hard to settle. I just can't relax. The uncertainty of it, the 'what if I did make a mistake,' it just gnaws and gnaws until I have to go look. So I suppose they are tangled up together, the mistake and the uncertainty, but it’s the sheer persistence of the thought that truly ruins my afternoon.
Is the feeling of uncertainty about whether something is in its place what drives you to check, rather than the fear of what might happen if you've made a mistake?

Well, yes, the uncertainty is a dreadful part of it, but... well, honestly, Doctor, it all just comes back to the checking. That's the real problem, isn't it? It's the checking that's ruining my days. As I was saying—and this is really the whole reason I'm sitting here in this chair today, the thing that finally made me realize I needed some help—what brought me in is that I find myself checking the exact same boxes out in the garage, the same lists I've made for myself, the same drawers in the condo, over and over and over again. 

I'll be looking right at the drawer, and I'll check it, and I know perfectly well I already looked. I can picture exactly what's inside it! But I just can't move on. I have to do it again. And the fear of a mistake, or the uncertainty... it all just culminates in this absolute need to look one more time before my brain will let me move on to the next task. 

And, oh, it's just so hard on Helen. She’ll be standing by the door, all ready to go out, perhaps we had plans to go to the botanical gardens or just to the market, and she’s just waiting for me to leave it be. She's standing there, and I'm standing there opening a drawer for the fourth time, and I know I'm holding us up, but I just can't stop myself. I have to check before I can walk away. So whether it's the uncertainty or the fear of a mistake, the end result is always me, stuck there, checking the same things repeatedly while my poor wife waits.
Is it the fear of having made a mistake that drives you to check these things, or is it the uncertainty of not knowing if everything is in its place?

Well, Doctor, I feel like we might be splitting hairs a bit here, because whether you want to label it as a fear of making a mistake or just the pure, agonizing uncertainty of it all, it all leads back to the exact same place. And I know I keep repeating myself, but I really want to make sure you understand the reality of my days, because what brought me in—the whole reason I finally picked up the phone to make this appointment—is that I find myself checking those same boxes out in the garage, the daily lists I write out, the same condo drawers, just over and over and over again. 

It almost doesn't matter if it's fear or uncertainty driving the bus, because the destination is always me, stuck staring at a drawer, entirely unable to transition to the next part of my day. I have to check it again before I can move on. I simply cannot walk away. And the sheer ridiculousness of it all, the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind, is that I know perfectly well I already looked! I know it! I can picture the contents of the drawer perfectly. But I just can't stop, even when my wife is standing right there in the hallway, purse in hand, just waiting for me to just leave it be so we can get on with our afternoon. So, you see, you can call it a fear of a mistake, or you can call it the uncertainty of not knowing, but the real issue, the thing that is completely exhausting me and holding up poor Helen, is the checking itself.
Do you feel like you're checking these things to regain a sense of control, or is it more about easing your uncertainty?

Well, Doctor, it's... I suppose it's a bit of both, isn't it? Control and uncertainty, they sort of dance around each other in my mind. But honestly, as I've been trying to explain, and I feel like a broken record here, it really just comes down to the act itself. The checking. That's the crux of it all. 

I mean, whether I'm trying to feel in control or just trying to quiet that awful nagging uncertainty, the result is exactly the same. I'm still out in the garage, opening and closing the same cardboard boxes of old teaching materials, or I'm standing in the kitchen staring at the daily to-do lists I write out on those little yellow legal pads, or I'm pulling open the same drawers in the condo. Over and over and over. 

And the thing that just absolutely confounds me—the thing that makes me feel like an utter fool—is that I *know* I've already looked! I have the memory of looking just moments prior! I can close my eyes and see the exact arrangement of the pens and the tape in the drawer, but my brain simply refuses to let me move on to the next part of my day until I look again. I just cannot transition. I'm stuck. 

And as I mentioned, poor Helen... she bears the brunt of it. She'll be standing right there, coat on, keys in hand, ready to head out to the grocery store or to visit our daughter, and she's just waiting. She's waiting for me to just leave it be. And I want to! I desperately want to just close the drawer and walk out the door with her, but I can't. I have to check it one more time. So, control or uncertainty, whichever it is, it's the checking that brought me to your office today.
Is your need to check things repeatedly more about fearing you've made a mistake or not knowing if everything is where it should be?

Well, Doctor, you know, we keep coming back to this idea of why I do it—whether it's the fear of a mistake or the uncertainty of it all—and I have to be honest, I'm really not sure how to parse that out anymore. I don't know if I can give you a clear answer on whether it's one or the other, because to me, it's all just a big, tangled mess in my head. 

I mean, maybe it's fear? Maybe it's not knowing? But honestly, when I'm standing there, staring at the drawer, I'm not thinking, "Oh, I'm afraid I made a mistake," or "Oh, I'm uncertain about the placement of this stapler." I'm just thinking that I absolutely, positively cannot step away until I look again. 

And I know I've said this a dozen times already today, but that's really the heart of the matter. It's the action itself. The checking. The boxes in the garage, the lists, the drawers... it's all the same. I just get stuck. And I know I've already checked, I know what's in there, but my brain just hits a wall and won't let me transition to whatever I'm supposed to be doing next. And there's Helen, bless her heart, just waiting and waiting while I'm trapped in this loop. So, fear or uncertainty... I just don't know. I really don't. I just know that I can't stop checking, and that's what I need help with.
Is the primary reason you check things repeatedly because you fear you might have made a mistake or because you are uncertain about whether everything is in its correct place?

Doctor, I... well, forgive an old man for saying so, but I feel like we are going around in circles here. You keep asking me to choose between the fear of a mistake and the uncertainty of it all, and I... I really just don't have a different answer to give you. I simply don't know. 

I've sat here and racked my brain trying to figure out how to give you the exact distinction you're looking for, but the truth is, it's like trying to untangle a knot where all the strings are the exact same color. When I'm standing there at the drawer in the condo, my mind isn't neatly categorizing my motives. It's not saying, "Ah, here is the fear," or "Here is the uncertainty." It's just... a wall. A complete, impenetrable wall that stops me from moving on with my day. 

I mean, I spent my whole career trying to be precise, making sure everything was just so, and now in my retirement, I can't even tell you why I'm stuck opening and closing a cardboard box of old files in my own garage. Helen will be standing by the door, jingling the car keys, and she'll say to me, "What are you looking for?" And I can't even tell her! I just tell her I need another minute. And then another minute. And then another. Because I know I already checked the yellow legal pad, I know what I wrote down for the day, but I just can't walk away. 

So if you're looking for me to pick one—fear or uncertainty—I really can't. I don't have that answer for you, no matter how many times we turn the question over. All I know is the checking itself, the endless, exhausting loop of it, and how much of our time it's wasting. I just want to know how to stop doing it.
Is your need to check things repeatedly driven more by the fear of having made a mistake or by the uncertainty of not knowing if everything is where it should be?

Doctor, I... well, are you testing my memory, or is this some sort of psychological tactic? Because unless I am losing my mind entirely, which I certainly hope I'm not at seventy-six, I believe this is the exact same question we've been wrestling with for the last ten minutes. And I... I really must apologize if I'm being obtuse, but I simply cannot give you a different answer than the one I've already given. I don't know. I truly, honestly do not know. 

I know you have your medical background, and I'm sure in your textbooks there is a very neat, tidy little line drawn between a 'fear of a mistake' and 'uncertainty'. But out there in the real world, in my condo, when I'm standing over those yellow legal pads or staring into the garage boxes... there is no line. It’s just a feeling of being completely paralyzed. I spent my entire career in education, standing in front of classrooms, trying to explain complex things clearly to my students, so it is incredibly frustrating for me to sit here and not be able to articulate the workings of my own mind to you. But I can't. 

When I'm stuck there, and poor Helen is sighing by the front door with her coat on, I am not weighing whether I'm afraid I wrote the wrong thing down or if I'm just uncertain the pad is centered on the counter. I am just... stuck. The engine is running but the car won't go into gear. So, if you need me to check a box on your clipboard that says 'fear' or a box that says 'uncertainty,' I'm afraid I'm going to have to leave them both blank. I just don't have that answer for you, Doctor, no matter how many different ways we try to approach it.
Is your repeated checking of things primarily due to a fear that you might have made an error?

Doctor, I... well, I'm starting to think you might be pulling my leg a little bit here. Are we... are we stuck in our own little loop now? Because, as I've been saying—and I really do apologize if I'm not giving you the textbook answer you need for your notes—I just cannot tell you if it's a fear of an error. 

I mean, I look back on my life, you know, all those years teaching, grading papers, making sure the lesson plans were exactly right. You had to be precise. You didn't want to make an error then, because the students relied on you. So maybe there's some lingering ghost of that? But when I'm standing in the kitchen, and my hand is on the drawer pull for the fifth time, and Helen is calling out to ask if I'm ready to leave... I'm not thinking about errors. I'm not thinking, "Oh, did I make a mistake?" I'm just thinking that my brain is demanding I look at the drawer again. 

It’s so frustrating, Doctor. It really is. Because I want to give you a clear answer. I want to say, "Yes, it's because I'm terrified I made an error," or "No, it's just this vague uncertainty." But I can't. It's just a compulsion. A wall. A complete inability to just walk away and get in the car with my wife. So... I'm sorry, but I just don't know if it's about an error. I really don't.
Do you feel like checking these things repeatedly gives you a sense of being in control of your life?

Control? Oh, my... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, Doctor, if anything, it feels like the exact opposite of control. It feels like I'm completely at the mercy of... well, of whatever this is. 

You see, when I was working, when I was teaching... I had control then. I had my classroom, I had my syllabus, I had a schedule that dictated Monday through Friday, eight to three-thirty. I knew exactly what was expected of me, and I knew what I expected of my students. That was control. And I suppose someone could look at my situation and say, well, now that I'm retired, maybe I'm grasping for some of that structure back? I've read articles in the Sunday paper about retirees struggling with the loss of routine, you know, men my age who suddenly don't know what to do with their hands or their time once the pension kicks in. 

But this checking... looking at that yellow legal pad over and over, or opening that cardboard box in the garage when I know perfectly well what's inside it... it doesn't make me feel like the captain of the ship. It makes me feel like a prisoner in my own home. I mean, if I were in control, I would just walk away! I would say to myself, "Alright, you've checked the drawer, now go get in the car with Helen." We like to go to the early dinner at this little Italian place down the road on Tuesdays, and I can't tell you how many times we've almost missed it entirely because I'm stuck in the kitchen, opening and shutting a drawer. 

So, no, it doesn't give me a sense of control. It's a complete loss of it. My brain says "stay here and look again," and my body just obeys, even though the rational part of me—the part of me that functioned perfectly well in society for decades—is screaming to just let it go. target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the motivation behind the checking behaviors (compulsions), whether it's to regain control or ease uncertainty. This directly relates to the purpose of the compulsions, which is covered under the Compulsions symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, Doctor, it's... I suppose it's a bit of both, isn't it? Control and uncertainty, they sort of dance around each other in my mind. But honestly, as I've been trying to explain, and I feel like a broken record here, it really just comes down to the act itself. The checking. That's the crux of it all. 

I mean, whether I'm trying to feel in control or just trying to quiet that awful nagging uncertainty, the result is exactly the same. I'm still out in the garage, opening and closing the same cardboard boxes of old teaching materials, or I'm standing in the kitchen staring at the daily to-do lists I write out on those little yellow legal pads, or I'm pulling open the same drawers in the condo. Over and over and over. 

And the thing that just absolutely confounds me—the thing that makes me feel like an utter fool—is that I *know* I've already looked! I have the memory of looking just moments prior! I can close my eyes and see the exact arrangement of the pens and the tape in the drawer, but my brain simply refuses to let me move on to the next part of my day until I look again. I just cannot transition. I'm stuck. 

And as I mentioned, poor Helen... she bears the brunt of it. She'll be standing right there, coat on, keys in hand, ready to head out to the grocery store or to visit our daughter, and she's just waiting. She's waiting for me to just leave it be. And I want to! I desperately want to just close the drawer and walk out the door with her, but I can't. I have to check it one more time. So, control or uncertainty, whichever it is, it's the checking that brought me to your office today.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking behavior is driven by a fear of making a mistake or the uncertainty of not knowing if everything is in its place
doctor.question: Is your need to check things repeatedly more about fearing you've made a mistake or not knowing if everything is where it should be?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking the same question (fear of mistake vs. uncertainty), which I have already answered multiple times by circling back to my chief complaint (compulsions/checking). My profile does not have a specific symptom distinguishing between fear of mistake vs. uncertainty, so I cannot provide a new symptom for this question.

patient.answer:
Well, Doctor, you know, we keep coming back to this idea of why I do it—whether it's the fear of a mistake or the uncertainty of it all—and I have to be honest, I'm really not sure how to parse that out anymore. I don't know if I can give you a clear answer on whether it's one or the other, because to me, it's all just a big, tangled mess in my head. 

I mean, maybe it's fear? Maybe it's not knowing? But honestly, when I'm standing there, staring at the drawer, I'm not thinking, "Oh, I'm afraid I made a mistake," or "Oh, I'm uncertain about the placement of this stapler." I'm just thinking that I absolutely, positively cannot step away until I look again. 

And I know I've said this a dozen times already today, but that's really the heart of the matter. It's the action itself. The checking. The boxes in the garage, the lists, the drawers... it's all the same. I just get stuck. And I know I've already checked, I know what's in there, but my brain just hits a wall and won't let me transition to whatever I'm supposed to be doing next. And there's Helen, bless her heart, just waiting and waiting while I'm trapped in this loop. So, fear or uncertainty... I just don't know. I really don't. I just know that I can't stop checking, and that's what I need help with.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking behavior is driven by a fear of making a mistake or the uncertainty of not knowing
doctor.question: Is the primary reason you check things repeatedly because you fear you might have made a mistake or because you are uncertain about whether everything is in its correct place?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking the exact same question (fear of mistake vs. uncertainty) that I have already answered multiple times by emphasizing the checking behavior (compulsions). The doctor is not asking about a new symptom from my profile, but rather re-asking a nuance about the motivation behind my compulsions, which I have already thoroughly addressed and deflected back to the compulsion itself.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... well, forgive an old man for saying so, but I feel like we are going around in circles here. You keep asking me to choose between the fear of a mistake and the uncertainty of it all, and I... I really just don't have a different answer to give you. I simply don't know. 

I've sat here and racked my brain trying to figure out how to give you the exact distinction you're looking for, but the truth is, it's like trying to untangle a knot where all the strings are the exact same color. When I'm standing there at the drawer in the condo, my mind isn't neatly categorizing my motives. It's not saying, "Ah, here is the fear," or "Here is the uncertainty." It's just... a wall. A complete, impenetrable wall that stops me from moving on with my day. 

I mean, I spent my whole career trying to be precise, making sure everything was just so, and now in my retirement, I can't even tell you why I'm stuck opening and closing a cardboard box of old files in my own garage. Helen will be standing by the door, jingling the car keys, and she'll say to me, "What are you looking for?" And I can't even tell her! I just tell her I need another minute. And then another minute. And then another. Because I know I already checked the yellow legal pad, I know what I wrote down for the day, but I just can't walk away. 

So if you're looking for me to pick one—fear or uncertainty—I really can't. I don't have that answer for you, no matter how many times we turn the question over. All I know is the checking itself, the endless, exhausting loop of it, and how much of our time it's wasting. I just want to know how to stop doing it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking behavior is driven by a fear of making a mistake or uncertainty about the placement of items
doctor.question: Is your need to check things repeatedly driven more by the fear of having made a mistake or by the uncertainty of not knowing if everything is where it should be?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking the same question about whether the checking is driven by fear of making a mistake or uncertainty. The patient has already addressed this multiple times, focusing on the compulsions (S066) and the inability to distinguish the underlying obsession. Since the question is exactly the same as the previous ones and asks for a distinction the patient cannot make (between two types of obsessions/motivations), and the patient has exhausted their explanation of S066, there is no new symptom profile to map this to, or rather, it's asking about the specific nature of the obsessions which the patient has repeatedly stated they cannot parse.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... well, are you testing my memory, or is this some sort of psychological tactic? Because unless I am losing my mind entirely, which I certainly hope I'm not at seventy-six, I believe this is the exact same question we've been wrestling with for the last ten minutes. And I... I really must apologize if I'm being obtuse, but I simply cannot give you a different answer than the one I've already given. I don't know. I truly, honestly do not know. 

I know you have your medical background, and I'm sure in your textbooks there is a very neat, tidy little line drawn between a 'fear of a mistake' and 'uncertainty'. But out there in the real world, in my condo, when I'm standing over those yellow legal pads or staring into the garage boxes... there is no line. It’s just a feeling of being completely paralyzed. I spent my entire career in education, standing in front of classrooms, trying to explain complex things clearly to my students, so it is incredibly frustrating for me to sit here and not be able to articulate the workings of my own mind to you. But I can't. 

When I'm stuck there, and poor Helen is sighing by the front door with her coat on, I am not weighing whether I'm afraid I wrote the wrong thing down or if I'm just uncertain the pad is centered on the counter. I am just... stuck. The engine is running but the car won't go into gear. So, if you need me to check a box on your clipboard that says 'fear' or a box that says 'uncertainty,' I'm afraid I'm going to have to leave them both blank. I just don't have that answer for you, Doctor, no matter how many different ways we try to approach it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's checking behavior is driven by a fear of making a mistake or uncertainty about the placement of items
doctor.question: Is your repeated checking of things primarily due to a fear that you might have made an error?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking the exact same question again (whether the checking is due to fear of making an error), which the patient has already repeatedly stated they cannot answer and is not covered as a distinct motivation in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... well, I'm starting to think you might be pulling my leg a little bit here. Are we... are we stuck in our own little loop now? Because, as I've been saying—and I really do apologize if I'm not giving you the textbook answer you need for your notes—I just cannot tell you if it's a fear of an error. 

I mean, I look back on my life, you know, all those years teaching, grading papers, making sure the lesson plans were exactly right. You had to be precise. You didn't want to make an error then, because the students relied on you. So maybe there's some lingering ghost of that? But when I'm standing in the kitchen, and my hand is on the drawer pull for the fifth time, and Helen is calling out to ask if I'm ready to leave... I'm not thinking about errors. I'm not thinking, "Oh, did I make a mistake?" I'm just thinking that my brain is demanding I look at the drawer again. 

It’s so frustrating, Doctor. It really is. Because I want to give you a clear answer. I want to say, "Yes, it's because I'm terrified I made an error," or "No, it's just this vague uncertainty." But I can't. It's just a compulsion. A wall. A complete inability to just walk away and get in the car with my wife. So... I'm sorry, but I just don't know if it's about an error. I really don't.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's repeated checking is driven by a need for control
doctor.question: Do you feel like checking these things repeatedly gives you a sense of being in control of your life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the checking behavior provides a sense of control, which is an inquiry into the psychological motivation or secondary gain of the compulsions, rather than the core symptoms of obsessions, compulsions, or functional impairment as defined in the profile.

patient.answer:
Control? Oh, my... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, Doctor, if anything, it feels like the exact opposite of control. It feels like I'm completely at the mercy of... well, of whatever this is. 

You see, when I was working, when I was teaching... I had control then. I had my classroom, I had my syllabus, I had a schedule that dictated Monday through Friday, eight to three-thirty. I knew exactly what was expected of me, and I knew what I expected of my students. That was control. And I suppose someone could look at my situation and say, well, now that I'm retired, maybe I'm grasping for some of that structure back? I've read articles in the Sunday paper about retirees struggling with the loss of routine, you know, men my age who suddenly don't know what to do with their hands or their time once the pension kicks in. 

But this checking... looking at that yellow legal pad over and over, or opening that cardboard box in the garage when I know perfectly well what's inside it... it doesn't make me feel like the captain of the ship. It makes me feel like a prisoner in my own home. I mean, if I were in control, I would just walk away! I would say to myself, "Alright, you've checked the drawer, now go get in the car with Helen." We like to go to the early dinner at this little Italian place down the road on Tuesdays, and I can't tell you how many times we've almost missed it entirely because I'm stuck in the kitchen, opening and shutting a drawer. 

So, no, it doesn't give me a sense of control. It's a complete loss of it. My brain says "stay here and look again," and my body just obeys, even though the rational part of me—the part of me that functioned perfectly well in society for decades—is screaming to just let it go. It's incredibly humiliating, to be completely honest with you. To be seventy-six years old and held hostage by a drawer or a piece of paper. If it's supposed to make me feel in control of my life, it is doing a absolutely terrible job of it.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of repeatedly checking things due to persistent thoughts of potentially misplacing or throwing away something important, despite knowing it's unlikely, align with the diagnostic criteria for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) with predominantly obsessive symptoms.
